sec.p: As shown in Figure 4a,c,d, the macro target-wise Spearman correlation in Broad-94 was 0.1518 (95% lineage-stratified bootstrap CI, 0.1019–0.2006). Eighteen of 20 target correlations were positive, and the median target correlation was 0.1628. The Broad-94 macro correlation was 0.2576 lower than the locked 2D holdout value. In the within-lineage permutation analysis, an association at least as large as the observed value occurred rarely (one-sided p = 0.00080), supporting partial but attenuated transfer of rank information.

The lineage-adjusted macro Spearman correlation was 0.1080, whereas the lineage-only reference yielded 0.0951. The paired expression-only-minus-lineage-only difference was +0.0567 (95% CI, 0.0040–0.1106). Thus, lineage composition did not fully explain the exploratory association, although it accounted for part of the observed signal.

At the target level, the highest correlations were observed for ERBB3 (ρ = 0.3489), CCNE1 (ρ = 0.3456), CTNNB1 (ρ = 0.3009), E2F3 (ρ = 0.2679), and YAP1 (ρ = 0.2614) (Figure 4b; Table S12). MAPK1 (ρ = −0.0307) and STK11 (ρ = −0.1010) were the only targets with negative correlations. After adjustment of the 20 target-level permutation p values, no target met the Benjamini–Hochberg FDR threshold of q < 0.05; the lowest adjusted value was q = 0.0640 for CCNE1. Accordingly, Broad-94 was interpreted at the fixed-panel level rather than as confirmatory evidence for individual targets.

Among lineage groups containing at least seven models, macro correlations ranged from −0.0099 to 0.2786. Leave-one-lineage-out estimates ranged from 0.1202 to 0.1832, and the pooled association remained positive after every lineage exclusion. The original estimates used model-level resampling. The subsequent donor audit and sensitivity analyses below address the identified shared donor, while retaining uncertainty about unresolved donor relationships.

The donor audit identified one confirmed same-donor pair among 25 models with donor information; 69 models remained unresolved (Table S22). Omitting ACH-002883 or ACH-002884 gave macro target-wise correlations of 0.1516 and 0.1539, respectively, compared with the original 0.1518. Under the conditional full-cohort bootstrap, the expression-only estimate was 0.1518 (0.1009 to 0.2007) and its paired difference from lineage-only prediction was 0.0567 (0.0027 to 0.1081) (estimate and 95% CI; Table S23). These findings quantify sensitivity to the identified pair, conditional on treating the unresolved models as separate units.

In the 25-model donor-documented subset, the expression-only macro correlation was 0.0741 (−0.0154 to 0.1618), with an expression-minus-lineage difference of −0.0571 (−0.1502 to 0.0305) under source-specific donor-cluster resampling. Both intervals included zero, so this subset did not establish superiority over lineage. Averaging the vectors within the 24 source-specific donor groups gave 0.0727 (−0.0195 to 0.1629) for expression-only prediction. This subset is not a representative replacement for Broad-94; changes relative to the full cohort can reflect sample and lineage composition as well as grouping. Paired within-subset model-versus-cluster intervals and secondary ranking sensitivities are provided in Tables S23 and S24. Incomplete donor ascertainment prevents these analyses from verifying full-cohort independence or providing a fully donor-adjusted effective sample size.

sec.title: 3.4. Blinded Independent External Validation in Sanger-148 Organoids
sec.p: The outcome-blinded Sanger eligibility pool comprised 162 organoids from 157 donors with both RNA-seq profiles and quality-controlled CRISPR screening records. After excluding 13 Broad-linked organoids and one additional organoid from the same donor as a Broad-linked model, the independent validation cohort contained 148 organoids from 144 unique donors. Of the 3845 unique locked expression features used across the 20 target models, 3790 were measured in the Sanger matrix; target-specific coverage ranged from 291 to 300 of 300 features (97.0–100%). The 148 × 20 blind prediction matrix and the associated manifests were SHA-256 sealed before CRISPR LFC outcomes were accessed, and all 11 prespecified pre-outcome seal checks passed. Panel-wide validation, target-level results, and robustness analyses are summarized in Figure 5 and Table S13.

Fourteen organoids were excluded from 162 eligible organoids representing 157 donors, leaving 148 organoids from 144 donors. (b) Panel-wide expression-only, lineage-only, and paired-difference estimates; error bars show 95% donor-cluster bootstrap confidence intervals. (c) Target-specific Spearman correlations with 95% confidence intervals. Blue points denote Benjamini–Hochberg q < 0.05; the dotted line denotes the macro correlation. (d) Robustness and tumor-type subgroup estimates. Predictions were SHA-256-sealed before outcome access; the primary macro correlation was 0.1015, 17/20 target estimates were positive, and the two-sided within-tumor-type donor-level permutation p-value was 0.00040. In (a), arrows indicate cohort selection. In (b), blue, gray, and orange points and error bars denote expression-only, lineage-only, and expression-minus-lineage estimates, respectively. In (c), gray points denote q ≥ 0.05, and error bars use the corresponding point colors. In (d), filled circles denote cohort-level estimates, with the primary estimate in blue and the sensitivity and lineage-only reference estimates in gray; open squares denote tumor-type subgroup estimates. Black dashed vertical lines in (b–d) mark zero. BH, Benjamini–Hochberg; CI, confidence interval; SHA-256, 256-bit Secure Hash Algorithm.

sec.p: As shown in Figure 5a,b, the frozen expression-only model achieved a macro target-wise Spearman correlation of 0.1015 in the independent Sanger-148 cohort (95% CI, 0.0637–0.1357). Seventeen of the 20 target estimates were positive. After repeated organoids were averaged within donors, 5000 two-sided permutations of complete 20-target outcome vectors within tumor-type strata yielded p = 0.00040. Thus, the locked 2D model carried a detectable rank-ordering signal into the independent 3D cohort, although the effect size was modest.

As shown in Figure 5c and Table S13, the largest target-specific correlations were observed for CDK6 (ρ = 0.3221; 95% CI, 0.1666–0.4702), MDM4 (ρ = 0.2992; 95% CI, 0.1483–0.4410), KEAP1 (ρ = 0.2967; 95% CI, 0.1256–0.4464), CTNNB1 (ρ = 0.2831; 95% CI, 0.1031–0.4563), and CCNE1 (ρ = 0.2792; 95% CI, 0.1014–0.4493). After Benjamini–Hochberg correction of the 20 target-level permutation p-values, only CDK6, MDM4, and CCNE1 met q < 0.05 (q = 0.0040 for each). CCND3, EGFR, and NFE2L2 were the three targets with negative correlations; no targets were removed based on direction or significance.

The tumor-type-adjusted macro Spearman correlation was 0.0882, whereas the frozen lineage-only reference achieved 0.0553 (95% CI, 0.0168–0.0917). The expression-only-minus-lineage difference was +0.0462, but its paired donor-cluster bootstrap interval included zero (95% CI, −0.0065 to 0.0986). The primary target-wise endpoint therefore did not establish superiority beyond tumor-origin information. The one-model-per-donor estimate (ρ = 0.1014) and donor-mean estimate (ρ = 0.0990) closely matched the primary result. Tumor-type subgroup estimates were 0.1030 for colorectal, 0.0654 for esophageal, 0.1755 for ovarian, 0.0300 for pancreatic, and 0.1500 for gastric organoids (Figure 5d). Ovarian results were exploratory, whereas pancreatic and gastric estimates were descriptive because of their small sample sizes.

An independent replay reproduced the cohort composition, target and prediction order, feature coverage, primary and sensitivity statistics, lock records, and file hashes, with all 22 predefined checks passing. No model retraining, target or feature selection, hyperparameter adjustment, or change to the prespecified primary metric occurred after the Sanger outcomes were opened. The retrospective within-organoid endpoints are reported separately in Section 3.7. These findings support a statistically detectable but quantitatively modest independent 3D rank-transfer signal, with the strongest target-level support for CDK6, MDM4, and CCNE1.

sec.title: 3.5. Retrospective Cross-Cohort Transportability Synthesis
sec.p: After the Broad-94 exploratory analysis and the Sanger-148 blinded external validation had been completed separately, their target-specific results were retrospectively combined for the unchanged 20-gene panel. The synthesis evaluated the direction and magnitude of rank transfer rather than the absolute agreement between the Broad Chronos Gene Effect and Sanger-corrected CRISPR LFC scales. Panel-wide and target-level synthesis results are summarized in Figure 6 and Table S14.

caption.p: Retrospective cross-cohort transportability synthesis across Broad-94 and Sanger-148 organoids. (a) Macro correlations for the locked 2D holdout, Broad-94, Sanger-148, and the fixed-effect combined 3D estimate. Error bars show cohort-specific 95% bootstrap confidence intervals and, for the combined 3D estimate, a descriptive 95% target-panel bootstrap interval. (b) Target-wise Broad-94 versus Sanger-148 correlations, classified as Tier A, B, or C. (c) Fixed-effect target-level meta-analytic correlations with 95% confidence intervals. (d) Evidence-tier counts and sensitivity summaries. The exact-binomial benchmark was descriptive, and the 50,000-iteration correlation-aware permutation was post hoc; neither constituted a new external validation. In (a), gray, green, purple, and brown points and error bars denote the locked 2D holdout, Broad-94, Sanger-148, and combined 3D estimates, respectively. In (b,c), blue circles, orange squares, and gray triangles denote Tiers A, B, and C, respectively; the same tier colors are used for the bars in (d). Solid black reference lines in (a–c) mark zero correlation. 2D, two-dimensional; 3D, three-dimensional; BH, Benjamini–Hochberg; CI, confidence interval.

sec.p: As shown in Figure 6a, the arithmetic mean of the 20 fixed-effect target-level meta-analytic correlations was 0.1231, with a 20,000-replicate target-panel bootstrap interval of 0.0769–0.1704. This combined 3D estimate was substantially lower than the locked 2D holdout correlation of 0.4094; the combined 3D-minus-locked-2D difference was −0.2863. The results therefore indicated measurable transfer of dependency ranking into organoids, accompanied by marked attenuation relative to performance within the 2D domain. This observed cross-domain performance contrast does not identify the biological or technical causes of attenuation.

Fifteen of the 20 frozen targets had positive correlations in both Broad-94 and Sanger-148 (75%). A one-sided exact binomial comparison against a null success probability of 0.50 yielded p = 0.0207. The targets were correlated, and we defined the synthesis after the cohort-specific results were known. We therefore interpreted this value only as a descriptive benchmark. In the post hoc correlation-aware sensitivity analysis, Sanger outcomes were first averaged within donors, and each unit’s complete 20-target outcome vector was permuted as a block. Fourteen of 20 targets remained positive in both cohorts, and 50,000 simultaneous permutations yielded a one-sided empirical p = 1.0 × 10−4 (Figure 6d).

As shown in Figure 6b,c and Table S14, eight targets met the combined meta-analytic Benjamini–Hochberg threshold of q < 0.05. The reporting classification comprised three Tier A, 12 Tier B, and five Tier C targets. The strongest Tier A support was observed for CCNE1 (Broad ρ = 0.3456; Sanger ρ = 0.2792; combined ρ = 0.3128; 95% CI, 0.1865–0.4290; q = 5.18 × 10−5), CDK6 (0.2447; 0.3221; combined ρ = 0.2924; 95% CI, 0.1660–0.4094; q = 1.01 × 10−4), and MDM4 (0.2000; 0.2992; combined ρ = 0.2655; 95% CI, 0.1400–0.3825; q = 2.36 × 10−4). These targets combined positive transfer in both cohorts, multiplicity-adjusted meta-analytic support, and target-level FDR support in at least one individual cohort.

The correlation between the vectors of target-specific Broad and Sanger performance estimates was ρ = 0.2782 (two-sided p = 0.2350), indicating that panel-wide directional replication did not imply stable relative performance ordering across cohorts (Figure 6b). The expression-only-minus-lineage differences were positive at the panel level in Broad-94 (one-sided Wilcoxon p = 0.0379) but did not reach the corresponding threshold in Sanger-148 (p = 0.1012). Thus, the retrospective synthesis strengthened evidence for limited cross-cohort directionality but did not constitute a third external validation or support equivalent target performance across the two organoid resources.

sec.title: 3.6. Secondary Transcriptomic Projection and Domain Diagnostics in Tiriac Pancreatic Organoids
sec.p: After completion of 2D model development, Broad-94 exploration, Sanger-148 validation, and retrospective synthesis, the same frozen expression-only deployment models were applied to the independent Tiriac pancreatic organoid RNA-seq cohort for secondary biological projection. The analysis included 55 samples: 44 tumor samples representing 38 independent tumor cases and 11 normal samples representing 11 independent normal cases. Of 3845 unique locked expression features, 3806 were observed (98.99%); target-specific coverage ranged from 292 to 300 of 300 features (97.33–100%), and all targets passed the prespecified 80% coverage gate. Because no measured genome-scale CRISPR dependency outcomes were available, these analyses evaluated model-output distributions and expression-domain shift rather than predictive accuracy. Figure 7 and Table S15 present model projections, not experimentally measured dependencies, together with expression-domain diagnostics.

caption.p: Model projections and expression-domain diagnostics in Tiriac pancreatic organoids. Panels (a–c) show model-predicted dependency scores, not experimentally measured dependencies. (a) Median projected Gene Effect across 38 tumor cases; blue hatched bars highlight CDK6, CCNE1, and MDM4, whereas gray bars represent the other targets. More negative values indicate stronger projected dependency within each model. (b) Tumor-minus-normal projection differences with 95% case-bootstrap confidence intervals; blue points and error bars indicate BH q < 0.05, whereas gray points and error bars indicate BH q ≥ 0.05; the vertical dashed line marks zero difference. (c) Tiriac tumor-median projections versus Broad-94 and Sanger-148 median predictions; the dashed line denotes numerical equality, not agreement with measured outcomes. (d) Expression-domain diagnostics: cumulative distributions of absolute SMD across 3790 shared features; dotted lines mark |SMD| = 1 and 2. Tiriac lacked measured CRISPR dependencies; these projections require experimental validation. BH, Benjamini–Hochberg; CI, confidence interval; CRISPR, clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats; SMD, standardized mean difference.

sec.p: As shown in Figure 7a, the most negative median projection among the 38 tumor cases was observed for CTNNB1 (−1.282), followed by CDK6 (−0.753), YAP1 (−0.481), BRAF (−0.435), and EGFR (−0.414). CTNNB1 and CDK6 ranked among the three most negative within-case projections in 37 of 38 tumor cases. Because each target was modeled separately, these values represent target-specific projected outputs rather than a common calibrated dependency scale.

Fifteen of the 20 tumor-normal model-output contrasts met Benjamini–Hochberg q < 0.05 (Figure 7b and Table S15). The largest tumor-directed difference was observed for CTNNB1 (tumor minus normal, −0.435; 95% bootstrap CI, −0.564 to −0.298; q = 0.00439). CDK6 also showed a more negative tumor projection (−0.200; 95% CI, −0.243 to −0.159; q = 2.09 × 10−5), and CCNE1 showed a smaller difference in the same direction (−0.027; 95% CI, −0.051 to −0.009; q = 0.0260). By contrast, MDM4 was more negative in normal cases (tumor minus normal, +0.245; 95% CI, +0.217 to +0.277; q = 1.17 × 10−5). These p and q values describe differences in frozen model outputs and do not demonstrate measured gene dependency or therapeutic sensitivity.

The 20-target median projection ranking in Tiriac tumor cases was concordant with the Broad-94 median prediction ranking (ρ = 0.717; two-sided p = 3.71 × 10−4) and the Sanger-148 median prediction ranking (ρ = 0.780; p = 4.91 × 10−5; Figure 7c). All three vectors were predictions from the same frozen model family, and Tiriac lacked measured CRISPR outcomes. These correlations therefore quantify target-hierarchy consistency rather than independent predictive accuracy.

Expression-domain diagnostics demonstrated substantial cohort shift. Across the 3790 frozen features shared by the three organoid resources, the median absolute SMD was 0.743 for Tiriac versus Broad-94 and 0.848 for Tiriac versus Sanger-148. The proportions with |SMD| > 1 were 38.7% and 43.4%, respectively, and the proportions with |SMD| > 2 were 13.2% and 14.6% (Figure 7d). PCA likewise separated the Tiriac samples from the Broad and Sanger cohorts. We reported these diagnostics without recalibration, feature deletion, target selection, or prediction modification. Accordingly, the Tiriac findings support secondary application and prioritization only, and we did not interpret them as validated dependencies.

Computational replay confirmed that the reference Tiriac projections used training-median imputation. Relative to these unchanged projections, zero filling produced a mean absolute change of 0.0114 and a maximum change of 0.1077 Gene Effect units; training-reference mean filling produced corresponding changes of 0.0017 and 0.0172. Across the 38 tumor-case profiles, mean within-profile Spearman agreement with the reference was 0.9771 for zero filling and 0.9991 for training-reference means. The top-three set was preserved in 36/38 and 38/38 tumor cases, respectively (Table S20). Zero filling therefore altered the short candidate list in two tumor cases despite high overall rank agreement.

The largest zero-fill shift occurred for RAF1 (−0.1077), whereas the largest training-reference mean shift occurred for CTNNB1 (−0.0172; Table S21). The tumor-median top-three hierarchy remained CTNNB1, CDK6 and YAP1 under both alternatives. Tumor–normal median differences and bootstrap limits changed by less than 0.000001; Mann–Whitney p-values, adjusted q-values, and the 15 significant projection contrasts were unchanged. This invariance follows from the common target-specific offsets in the linear models and does not independently validate the projections. The sensitivity analysis does not identify the most accurate imputation method because Tiriac lacks measured dependency outcomes.

The retrospective coverage-threshold check retained all 20 target models in each external cohort at 80%, 90%, and 95% (Table S16). Coverage was 100% in Broad-94, 97.0–100% in Sanger-148, and 97.33–100% in Tiriac. Because the threshold acts only as an eligibility gate and none of the models failed the stricter requirements, using 90% or 95% would leave the frozen predictions and their reported summaries unchanged.

sec.title: 3.7. Retrospective Gene Ranking Within Individual Organoids
sec.p: Using the unchanged 20-gene predictions, the mean within-organoid Spearman correlation was 0.3428 (95% CI, 0.3026 to 0.3826) in Broad-94 and 0.4294 (95% CI, 0.3926 to 0.4645) in Sanger-148 (Table S17). The corresponding fixed 2D-mean comparator estimates were 0.2057 and 0.1995. Paired expression-minus-fixed-mean differences were +0.1371 (95% CI, 0.0987 to 0.1780) and +0.2299 (95% CI, 0.1981 to 0.2613), respectively. These estimates address gene ordering within each organoid and are not directly comparable to the original macro target-wise correlations of 0.1518 and 0.1015.

The archived lineage-only predictions yielded mean within-organoid correlations of 0.2745 in Broad and 0.3884 in Sanger. Expression-minus-lineage differences were +0.0684 (95% CI, 0.0334 to 0.1032) and +0.0411 (95% CI, 0.0167 to 0.0656), respectively. Thus, full-panel gene ranking showed a modest retrospective gain over lineage-only prediction in both cohorts (Table S17). This finding does not change the uncertainty in the original Sanger target-wise expression-minus-lineage difference.

Top-three overlap was 34.04% in Broad and 42.79% in Sanger, compared with 34.75% and 35.36% for lineage-only prediction (Table S18). Paired expression-minus-lineage differences were −0.71 percentage points (95% CI, −4.96 to 3.19) in Broad and +7.43 percentage points (95% CI, 4.28 to 10.74) in Sanger. The Broad interval included zero; superiority for selecting the three strongest measured dependencies was therefore not demonstrated across both cohorts.

Averaging the 20-gene vectors within each Sanger donor before evaluation gave a mean within-donor correlation of 0.4338 (95% CI, 0.3986 to 0.4675). The paired difference from lineage-only prediction was +0.0402 (95% CI, 0.0157 to 0.0652). Mean top-three overlap was 42.82%, with an expression-minus-lineage difference of +6.94 percentage points (95% CI, 4.17 to 9.95; Table S19). These results were consistent with the organoid-weighted analysis. All within-organoid findings remain retrospective and restricted to the selected 20-gene panel.

sec.title: 4. Discussion
sec.p: This study tested whether transcriptome-based gene-dependency rankings learned in 2D cancer models retained a detectable but attenuated signal in patient-derived 3D organoids. Transfer was evaluated without outcome-guided retraining. The findings provide limited support for this hypothesis. We selected the expression-only representation in the development cohort. Holdout performance provided internal confirmation conditional on historical target selection. Positive panel-wide rank signals were observed in the Broad-94 exploratory cohort and the Sanger-148 blinded independent external validation cohort. However, macro correlations in Broad, Sanger, and the combined 3D analysis were markedly lower than in the locked 2D holdout. Transfer was therefore incomplete and weak. The findings support modest, context-sensitive preservation of organoid ranking for genes within the preselected panel across independently generated resources. They do not establish cross-platform equivalence. This primary finding is distinct from the secondary within-organoid gene-ranking results in Section 3.7.

Tumor lineage is central to interpreting this transfer. Expression patterns can encode tissue identity and shared transcriptional programs. A model may therefore reproduce differences in dependency between tumor types without identifying the mechanisms responsible for those dependencies. The CRISPR outcomes measure gene-depletion effects, but the fitted expression–dependency relationships remain predictive associations. Their transfer does not establish that the predictive expression features have a causal role in determining dependency. Thus, predictive generalization to organoids and mechanistic generalization are distinct claims.

For the prespecified target-wise endpoint, the added predictive value of transcriptomic modeling over tumor lineage was not established in the blinded Sanger cohort. The expression-only model exceeded the frozen lineage-only comparator numerically by 0.0462 in macro Spearman correlation. However, the paired donor-cluster bootstrap CI included zero (95% CI, −0.0065 to 0.0986). This result establishes neither superiority nor equivalence. The significant within-lineage permutation result addresses a different question: whether the prediction–outcome association exceeds a null distribution that preserves tumor-type structure. It does not establish superior performance over the lineage-only predictor. Target-specific correlations rank organoids for a given gene. They cannot by themselves establish correct gene ranking within an organoid or an increase in the yield of functional experiments. The study contributes an outcome-blinded assessment of performance attenuation from cell lines to organoids and documents uncertainty in the incremental value of transcriptomic prediction. CDK6, MDM4, and CCNE1 remain candidates for prospective investigation. Their multiplicity-adjusted correlations do not establish target-specific superiority over lineage or practical benefit.

The retrospective within-organoid analysis directly examined this second ranking task. Full 20-gene rankings improved over a fixed 2D-mean ranking and, more modestly, over lineage-only prediction in both cohorts (Table S17). These comparisons are needed because shared differences in average dependency among genes can produce positive within-organoid correlations. A gain in full-panel correlation did not ensure a better short candidate list. Top-three overlap exceeded lineage-only prediction in Sanger but not in Broad (Table S18). The donor-mean sensitivity analysis gave similar Sanger results (Table S19). This is limited retrospective evidence of ranking agreement within a selected panel, not prospective proof that transcriptomic modeling improves experimental yield. It neither replaces the original primary analysis nor resolves its uncertainty about target-wise superiority over lineage.

Adding copy-number, mutation, and lineage information to gene expression did not reliably improve development performance. DeepDEP and transcriptome-based maps developed for The Cancer Genome Atlas use molecular profiles from cancer cell lines to estimate dependencies in functionally unscreened tumors [16,17]. Synthetic data augmentation and multi-omic integration have also been proposed to address incomplete profiles and capture more complex dependency patterns [18]. The expression-plus-copy-number candidate yielded the highest development score numerically. However, its advantage over expression-only was negligible, and the paired bootstrap interval included zero. The expression-only representation also showed the greatest feature-set stability and was selected by the prespecified one-standard-error rule. This result does not imply that copy number or mutation is biologically uninformative. This finding applies to the fixed 20-target panel, the available sample size, the 300-feature limit per target, and the linear Elastic Net framework. Within these constraints, the additional data layers did not provide a sufficiently stable incremental signal to justify greater complexity. The broad availability and relatively consistent measurement of transcriptomic data across model collections further strengthens the practical rationale for an expression-only deployment model.

Performance was lower in the organoid cohorts than in the 2D internal confirmation analysis. The macro Spearman correlation was 0.4094 in the locked 2D holdout, compared with 0.1518 in Broad-94 and 0.1015 in Sanger-148. This attenuation is interpreted as an observed cross-domain effect whose biological and technical causes remain uncertain. Computational alignment studies have documented transcriptional differences between cell lines and tumors [20]. Next-generation model resources have reported tumor-relevant transcriptional programs and culture-specific dependencies in organoids and spheroids [38], while patient-derived model collections have shown that culture conditions can modify cellular states in a subset of models [40]. These studies provide context for plausible explanations, but they do not establish the causes of the performance decline in the present cohorts. Differences in cellular state, growth geometry, medium composition, lineage composition, and functional-screening platforms may contribute individually or jointly. Their contributions were not experimentally disentangled or quantified here. The comparison used different cohorts and assay settings, rather than paired models in which growth conditions and screening platforms were varied under controlled conditions. It therefore cannot attribute the decline to 3D growth itself, identify a dominant mechanism, or exclude contributions from model limitations and cohort composition. Historical target-panel selection also limits interpretation of the 2D reference estimate. The observed attenuation supports evaluating dependency models across data domains without assigning a confirmed biological or technical explanation to the decline.

The contrasting roles of Broad-94 and Sanger-148 were central to the evidential interpretation. Broad-94 was retained as exploratory because the resource had been accessible during earlier methodological work and donor information was absent from the original evaluation records. The later audit recovered only partial donor information and confirmed a same-donor pair (Tables S22–S24); it did not establish independence of the full cohort. The audited analysis run nevertheless preserved a prediction-before-outcome sequence. Sanger-148, by contrast, was constructed after excluding Broad-linked and same-donor records, and its predictions were cryptographically sealed before the CRISPR outcomes were opened. Donor-clustered uncertainty estimation and donor-aware permutation further preserved the strongest available biological independence structure. Differences in screening libraries, protocols, and computational processing can affect Broad and Sanger dependency estimates [10,11]. Chronos was developed in part to model sources of variation in CRISPR screen dynamics [12]. Target-wise correlations were positive for 18 of 20 targets in Broad-94 and 17 of 20 in Sanger-148. This pattern suggests that the panel-wide direction was not confined to a single laboratory or processing system. Nevertheless, the Sanger target-wise expression-only-minus-lineage CI included zero, so that cohort did not establish an incremental advantage on the prespecified primary endpoint. Transcriptomic information therefore carried a detectable external rank signal, but part of that signal may reflect lineage-associated structure.

The target-level findings provided the strongest cross-cohort support for CCNE1, CDK6, and MDM4. CCNE1 was positive in both organoid cohorts, passed the FDR threshold in Sanger-148, and yielded one of the largest combined estimates. This is biologically consistent with the recent Sanger organoid dependency map, in which CCNE1 amplification in esophageal organoids was associated with CCNE1 dependency [39]. CDK6 produced the highest target-specific correlation in Sanger-148 and remained in Tier A in the retrospective synthesis. The Broad NextGen study reported enrichment for CDK6 dependency in glioblastoma models that preserve a tumor-proximal glial transcriptional state. Genetic and pharmacological experiments supported this association in specific genomic contexts [38]. That work provides an example of how transcriptional state can expose context-dependent CDK6 vulnerability. MDM4 also showed a positive ranking signal in both cohorts. However, the current reference set provides less direct organoid-based mechanistic support for MDM4 than for CCNE1 or CDK6. MDM4 should therefore be regarded primarily as a hypothesis for targeted functional testing. These findings identify genes whose variation across organoids was predicted with the strongest support. They do not establish that these are the three strongest dependencies within an individual organoid. More generally, their target-specific correlations do not demonstrate drug sensitivity, therapeutic index, or clinical benefit.

The retrospective synthesis distinguished directional replication at the panel level from stability in the relative ordering of target performance. Fifteen of the 20 targets were positive in both cohorts. The directionally concordant count remained above the correlation-aware null expectation when complete target vectors were permuted as blocks. In contrast, the correlation between the Broad and Sanger vectors of target-specific performance was only 0.2782 and was not statistically significant. Most targets therefore transferred in the same direction. This does not imply that they were predicted with equivalent strength in both organoid resources. The Tier A–C framework summarized these differences. Tier A identified the three targets with replicated direction, combined multiplicity-adjusted support, and individual-cohort evidence. Tier B captured directionally concordant but less strongly supported signals. Tier C indicated non-positive transfer in at least one cohort. Because these tiers were assigned retrospectively after the cohort-specific results were known, they should be treated as reporting categories rather than validated biological classes. Their reproducibility must be tested prospectively in a new cohort using prespecified criteria.

The Tiriac pancreatic organoid analysis provided a complementary application layer rather than an additional validation experiment. Pancreatic organoids have been shown to preserve important disease features and treatment-response patterns [30,31,32,33]. The Tiriac tumor-case target ranking was concordant with the median prediction rankings in Broad and Sanger. Thus, the frozen model family produced a broadly consistent target hierarchy in an independent pancreatic transcriptomic resource. However, all compared values were predictions from the same model family, and Tiriac provided no measured genome-scale CRISPR outcomes. The observed concordance therefore reflects cross-cohort consistency of model outputs, not predictive accuracy. Moreover, principal component separation and large SMDs across the shared expression features indicated substantial domain shift. CTNNB1 had the most negative pancreatic projection but was not a Tier A target in the CRISPR synthesis. MDM4 was projected to be more negative in normal than tumor cases. These findings further illustrate why the outputs should not be interpreted as a context-independent hierarchy of biological dependency.

The retrospective missing-feature sensitivity analysis showed high overall agreement with the original median-imputed Tiriac projections. However, zero filling changed the top-three set in two of 38 tumor cases, and individual target shifts reached 0.1077 Gene Effect units. Training-reference mean filling preserved all tumor-case top-three sets, but this agreement cannot establish greater accuracy. Constant per-target offsets explain the unchanged tumor–normal contrasts. These findings support reporting the preprocessing rule explicitly and retaining the projections as hypotheses for functional testing (Tables S20 and S21).

The computational framework may help select direct organoid experiments, but its utility requires prospective testing. Genome-scale or large-scale CRISPR studies in intestinal, colon, and gastric organoids have identified context-specific genes related to growth, treatment resistance, and gene-drug interactions [34,35,36,37]. The larger Sanger organoid biobank has likewise mapped dependencies linked to genomic and clinical features through direct perturbation [39]. Such experiments provide stronger evidence of functional causality than computational projections, but remain technically demanding and resource-intensive. Frozen expression models could be evaluated as a low-cost pre-screen for allocating scarce CRISPR or pharmacological validation capacity. The within-organoid analysis tests the relative ordering of measured scores within 20 genes. It does not establish a common calibrated dependency scale across independently fitted gene models. Its modest full-ranking gains and cohort-dependent top-three results require prospective confirmation before claiming improved target prioritization.

Several design features strengthen the study. Patient-grouped nested cross-validation reduced leakage between biologically related samples. The one-standard-error rule limited unnecessary complexity when candidate performance was nearly equivalent [22,23]. The locked 2D evaluation, the subsequent all-852 deployment refit, the Broad exploratory application, and the Sanger blinded external validation were kept analytically distinct. Targets, feature identities, hyperparameters, and the primary metric were not reopened in response to 3D outcomes. Prediction-before-outcome locks, SHA-256 manifests, independent computational replay, and bootstrap and permutation schemes matched to the available biological unit reduced opportunities for retrospective optimization. Retaining all 20 targets irrespective of effect direction or statistical significance also reduced selective reporting. The accompanying reproducibility package allows readers to trace the reported results to frozen predictions, analysis records, and integrity checks.

The study also has important limitations. First, historical selection of the fixed 20-gene panel used all 852 2D models. The 171-model holdout was independent of the current candidate representation, feature selection, hyperparameters, and model-fitting decisions. However, it was not fully independent of historical target selection. The holdout therefore provides internal confirmation conditional on that selection, not an unbiased estimate of generalization for the complete analysis pipeline. Selection-induced optimism cannot be excluded or quantified by the reported fixed-panel analysis. Second, all external performance estimates are restricted to the preselected 20 targets. Sample independence in Sanger does not establish dependency transferability for unselected genes or across the genome. Target-panel bootstrap intervals quantify sensitivity to panel composition rather than sampling uncertainty for new patients or organoids. Third, donor metadata could be recovered for only 25 of the 94 Broad models, and one same-donor pair was confirmed. The remaining 69 models and cross-source donor equivalence could not be resolved. The partial-cluster and donor-documented-subset sensitivities do not establish full-cohort independence. Original Broad CIs, permutation results and the uncertainty weights used in retrospective synthesis remain conditional on model-level independence and may overstate precision if additional dependence is present. Consequently, Broad and Sanger uncertainty estimates and effective sample sizes are not directly comparable. Fourth, Sanger-148 was dominated by colorectal and esophageal organoids. Ovarian, pancreatic, and gastric subgroups were too small to establish lineage-specific generalizability. Fifth, the differing Broad Chronos Gene Effect and Sanger-corrected LFC scales precluded direct absolute-error and calibration comparisons [10,11,12]. Sixth, target-specific linear expression-only models cannot fully represent genotype-transcriptome interactions, network structure, cell–cell interactions, or the incompletely modeled stromal and immune compartments of organoid systems [24,25,29]. Finally, the Tiriac normal group contained only 11 cases and lacked measured CRISPR dependencies, matched drug-response outcomes, and clinical endpoints. The study consequently establishes rank-transfer evidence, not prospective therapeutic utility.

Adjustment for broad tumor-type labels and comparison with a lineage-only reference cannot fully separate lineage-associated transcriptional structure from other predictive signals. The present analyses therefore do not establish the causal basis of the transferred associations. Lineage adjustment and descriptive expression-domain diagnostics do not experimentally separate the causes of performance attenuation. The present design cannot estimate the individual contributions of culture conditions, cellular state, cohort composition, and screening technology to the observed cross-domain effect.

The within-organoid endpoints introduce additional limitations. They were specified retrospectively after outcomes were available, and their CIs were not adjusted for multiple secondary comparisons. The fixed panel and frozen-model analysis do not establish genome-wide ranking performance or quantify uncertainty from retraining or selecting a different gene panel. Additional same-donor dependence remains unresolved in Broad despite the partial-donor secondary ranking sensitivities in Table S24. Finally, agreement with CRISPR score ordering is not evidence of cancer selectivity, druggability, therapeutic benefit, or increased success of prospectively chosen experiments.

Future work should test the Tier A targets using direct CRISPR perturbation in preregistered, tumor-type-balanced organoid cohorts. Gene-depletion effects should be related to target-specific inhibitor responses and, where available, to matched clinical information. Distinguishing biological from technical contributions to attenuation would require larger cohorts with patient-level identifiers, paired 2D and 3D models, controlled variation in culture conditions, and harmonized or cross-platform CRISPR measurements. Nonlinear models incorporating network or pathway structure, domain-adaptation strategies, and richer multi-omic representations are also reasonable candidates for evaluation. Their value, however, should be assessed without outcome-guided retuning and under the same prediction-lock and independent-validation discipline used here. The results document modest rank transfer within the selected gene panel. Whether the retrospective within-organoid ranking gains improve prospective experimental prioritization beyond tumor lineage remains to be established.

sec.title: 5. Conclusions
sec.p: This study shows that transcriptome-based models learned in 2D cancer models retain a weak ability to rank patient-derived 3D organoids by dependency for genes in the preselected panel, without retraining and with substantial attenuation. More complex omic representations did not provide a reliable advantage over the expression-only model. Its macro Spearman correlation of 0.4094 in the locked 2D holdout provides internal confirmation conditional on historical target selection, not an unbiased generalization estimate. Performance decreased to 0.1518 in the Broad-94 exploratory cohort and to 0.1015 in the Sanger-148 blinded, independent external validation cohort. The Sanger association nevertheless exceeded the permutation-based null expectation. Eighteen of 20 target estimates were positive in Broad-94, 17 of 20 were positive in Sanger-148, and 15 of 20 were positive in both cohorts. The combined 3D macro correlation of 0.1231 therefore supports a modest, directionally reproducible rank-transfer signal rather than complete cross-system generalizability. The primary endpoint did not establish added predictive value beyond tumor lineage in Sanger. These results support transfer of predictive associations without establishing their causal basis. Broad uncertainty and retrospective pooled evidence remain conditional on incomplete donor ascertainment. The attenuation is an observed cross-domain effect; its biological and technical causes were not experimentally disentangled and remain uncertain.

CCNE1, CDK6, and MDM4 received the strongest cross-cohort support and represent priorities for direct functional investigation rather than established therapeutic sensitivities. The Tiriac pancreatic projection showed that the frozen models could be applied to an independent transcriptomic cohort while retaining aspects of the target hierarchy. However, measured CRISPR outcomes were unavailable, and expression-domain shift was substantial. These limitations preclude interpreting that analysis as validation. The separate retrospective within-organoid analysis showed modest gains over lineage-only prediction for full 20-gene rankings in both cohorts, but a top-three overlap gain only in Sanger. These findings provide limited evidence for ranking genes within the selected panel. They do not establish dependency transferability for unselected genes or at genome scale. Prospective experimental prioritization beyond tumor lineage remains unestablished. The computational approach does not replace direct organoid CRISPR screening, pharmacological validation, or assessment of clinical utility. Prospective evaluation in larger, tumor-type-balanced, preregistered organoid cohorts will be required to establish the biological robustness and translational value of the prioritized targets.

sec.title: Data Availability Statement
sec.p: This study analyzed publicly available or openly released datasets. The 2D molecular profiles and CRISPR Gene Effect data were obtained from the DepMap Public 26Q1 release and the CCLE [3,4,13,14] (https://depmap.org/portal/data_page/?tab=allData) (accessed on 26 September 2026). The Broad NextGen organoid data were obtained from the NextGen Model Manuscript 2026 resource and the associated Figshare dataset [38] (https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.29472362.v1). The Sanger tumor-derived organoid dependency data were obtained from the associated Figshare dataset [39] (https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.28339340). The Tiriac pancreatic organoid RNA-seq data were obtained from the GDC ORGANOID-PANCREATIC project [32] (https://portal.gdc.cancer.gov/projects/ORGANOID-PANCREATIC) (accessed on 26 September 2026). The analysis code, trained models, processed data, and supporting results are available in the study’s reproducibility repository on Zenodo [41]. Original source datasets remain available from their respective repositories under the applicable access and licensing conditions.
